title: How Technology, Geopolitics, and Energy Could Redraw the Global Manufacturing Map
gist: BCG Henderson Institute modeling of 54 countries and 47 industries finds the US, Western Europe and Japan could lose $1.8 trillion of manufacturing value added and 26 million jobs if cost gaps persist, but AI-driven factories of the future (up to 2.5x labor productivity) are the only force that could lift these hubs above today's output. Tariffs buy time but lose value (even turn negative) as productivity rises, and automation narrows but cannot erase energy-cost disadvantages, which AI data-center demand is itself worsening.

insights.claim: Since 2000, China's share of global manufacturing value added (MVA) has risen 28 percentage points and India's 2, while the US and Western Europe each lost 11 points and Japan 5.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Frames the structural share shift that any reshoring or industrial-policy thesis has to overcome.
insights.locator: The Evolution of Manufacturing Competitiveness

insights.claim: BCG Henderson Institute modeling estimates that if current cost disadvantages persist, about $1.8 trillion of MVA could move out of the US, Western Europe and Japan, putting roughly 26 million direct and indirect manufacturing jobs at risk.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Sizes the downside for industrial exposure in high-cost hubs absent modernization.
insights.locator: BCG Institute's modeling suggests that if these trends persist

insights.claim: Western Europe carries the largest share of at-risk manufacturing ($991 billion MVA, 15 million jobs), followed by the US ($460 billion, 5 million jobs) and Japan ($314 billion, 6 million jobs).
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Western European industrials are the most exposed to relocation risk; overweight caution there absent FoF investment.
insights.locator: Western Europe accounts for the largest share

insights.claim: In the US, Western Europe and Japan, manufacturing productivity has failed to keep pace with wage growth, and high energy prices in Europe and Japan have compounded the resulting cost disadvantage while China improved its ecosystem, infrastructure and workforce.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Wage-productivity gap plus energy cost is the mechanism driving hub erosion; watch both to judge reversal.
insights.locator: In traditional manufacturing hubs

themes.theme: Technology as the only reversing force

insights.claim: Across a model of 54 countries and 47 industries (over 95% of global MVA), technology is the only one of three forces—technology, tariffs, energy costs—that could lift the traditional hubs' combined MVA above today's level; tariffs and energy can only offset part of the losses.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Industrial-automation capex is a more durable reshoring lever than trade policy; position accordingly.
insights.quote: technology is the only force that could lift the traditional hubs’ MVA above today’s level
insights.locator: We modeled how the traditional hubs’ combined MVA would change

insights.claim: Agentic systems and physical AI can enable 'factories of the future' (FoF) delivering up to 2.5x the labor productivity of conventional factories, narrowing or reversing the cost advantage of lower-cost countries.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Supports demand for industrial AI, robotics and factory digitization vendors serving high-cost regions.
insights.locator: Recent breakthroughs in agentic systems and physical AI

insights.claim: The scope of manufacturing work that can be automated has expanded by 50% in just three years.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Rapidly widening automation addressable market for industrial robotics and software.
insights.quote: The scope of work that manufacturers can automate has expanded by 50% in just three years
insights.locator: The FoF has long promised to transform manufacturing

insights.claim: Widespread FoF adoption and full realization of gains in high-cost countries could take decades, but the productivity improvement could make upgrading an existing plant more economical than relocating abroad.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Long adoption horizon argues for patient, multi-decade exposure rather than near-term rerating.
insights.locator: Although it will take time—potentially decades

insights.claim: Under a radical fivefold labor-productivity scenario (80% less labor), the US, Western Europe and Japan could gain about $2.3 trillion MVA versus no productivity gain, with Western Europe gaining roughly $1,663 billion, the US $320 billion and Japan $275 billion.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Western Europe has the biggest upside optionality from extreme automation thanks to its infrastructure and skills base.
insights.locator: The results suggest how dramatically the manufacturing map could change

insights.claim: As automation cuts labor content, wage levels matter less for location decisions and qualitative factors such as infrastructure and workforce capabilities—where hubs like Western Europe remain strong—gain weight.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Location advantage shifts from cheap labor to skills and infrastructure; reassess low-wage-hub manufacturing plays.
insights.locator: As automation reduces the labor required

insights.claim: Realizing FoF productivity requires skilled workers, strong digital infrastructure, and the flexibility to reorganize operations and retrain employees, not just new technology.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Companies lacking digital and skills foundations may underdeliver on automation ROI.
insights.locator: Still, achieving the productivity gains from automation

themes.theme: Automation vs. logistics: where reshoring wins

insights.claim: Whether FoF makes high-cost-country production competitive depends on two factors: an industry's automation potential and the cost of transporting finished goods to customers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Screen sectors on automation potential x freight intensity to find reshoring winners.
insights.locator: The benefits are likely to vary considerably by industry

insights.claim: When the residual cost gap after automation is smaller than the logistics cost of importing from a lower-cost country, local production near customers becomes cheaper; where automation saves little and transport is cheap, offshore production keeps its advantage.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Heavy/bulky goods with high automation potential are the most likely candidates for onshoring.
insights.quote: When the remaining difference is smaller than the logistics costs of importing goods from a lower-cost country, manufacturing closer to customers becomes the cheaper option.
insights.locator: The benefits are likely to vary considerably by industry

themes.theme: Jobs: modernize or lose the factory

insights.claim: BCG argues the real choice for traditional hubs is not between today's employment and an automated future but between modernizing factories and losing them, since automation can preserve jobs that would otherwise move abroad.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Counters the automation-destroys-jobs narrative; supports political feasibility of pro-automation industrial policy.
insights.quote: the real choice facing these regions is not between today’s employment and an automated future, but between modernizing factories and losing them
insights.locator: How the Factory of the Future May Impact Jobs

insights.claim: Without productivity gains, Western Europe's direct and indirect manufacturing employment could fall from about 42 million to 27.6 million; with 2.5x productivity it reaches only 34.9 million, and only a fivefold gain restores it to about 40 million (40-45 million including jobs elsewhere in the economy).
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Even successful automation leaves European manufacturing employment below today; expect political pressure for support.
insights.locator: Our model of Western Europe illustrates the difference

insights.claim: Timing matters: if production relocates before hyperproductive factory technology is widely adopted it may never return, because reestablishing closed or relocated capacity is far harder than retaining it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Hysteresis risk means near-term relocation decisions are effectively permanent; early modernizers have an edge.
insights.quote: If production moves abroad before the technology is widely adopted, it may never return.
insights.locator: But the timing of deploying hyperproductive factories matters

insights.claim: Many factory jobs will disappear and others will shift toward supervising robotic systems, training robots and fixing problems automation cannot handle, requiring retraining on an industrial scale and hiring of AI expertise.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Creates demand for industrial reskilling, training and AI talent services.
insights.locator: And even when factories stay

insights.claim: Industrial policy measures motivated by economic security have increased more than sixfold since 2022, spanning tariffs, subsidies, export controls, investment screening and local-content rules, notably in semiconductors, metals and rare earths.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Policy intervention is a structural, rising factor in sectors like chips and critical minerals.
insights.locator: Governments today are intervening more actively

insights.claim: In a 2025 BCG Institute survey of 1,000 manufacturing executives, 90% said tariffs above 25% would make exporting uneconomical, and geopolitical risk ranked fourth among leading challenges, up from sixth in 2022.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: A ~25% tariff level is a practical threshold where trade flows break; watch tariff moves around it.
insights.quote: 90% said that tariffs above 25% would make exporting uneconomical
insights.locator: In a 2025 BCG Institute survey of 1,000 manufacturing executives

insights.claim: At today's productivity, high tariffs would retain about $688 billion of MVA in Western Europe, $552 billion in the US and $251 billion in Japan that would otherwise shift abroad under free trade.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much domestic output currently leans on protection and is exposed to tariff rollbacks.
insights.locator: Trade protection can help countries retain manufacturing activity

insights.claim: Protectionism raises costs for manufacturers and consumers, invites reciprocal measures that limit exports, reduces pressure to improve productivity, and may be short-lived as trade agreements and political priorities change.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Tariff-protected earnings are fragile and policy-dependent; discount them.
insights.locator: But policymakers must balance the benefits

insights.claim: As productivity rises, tariff value flips: in Western Europe tariff-protected MVA falls from $688 billion to about $465 billion with medium productivity gains, and with fivefold productivity high tariffs reduce potential MVA by $315 billion versus open trade, with similar patterns in the US and Japan.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Productive manufacturers gain more from open market access than protection; tariff escalation hurts automated exporters.
insights.locator: As factories become more productive, however

insights.claim: Persistent global trade imbalances may require a coordinated multilateral response, but countries can act unilaterally by investing in manufacturing technology.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Technology investment is a policy lever not hostage to trade negotiations.
insights.locator: The implications extend beyond tariffs themselves

themes.theme: Energy costs as a new dividing line

insights.claim: In 2025, Western European manufacturers paid roughly 2.5-3x as much for industrial electricity as US and Chinese manufacturers, with Western European prices up more than 50% since 2010, while Japanese manufacturers paid about twice as much.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Structural energy cost gap disadvantages European energy-intensive producers versus US and China peers.
insights.locator: Since 2010, industrial electricity has become more expensive

insights.claim: Industrial electricity has grown more expensive since 2010 because supply lagged demand, heavy grid investment was passed to users, and market rules designed for flat demand and falling costs pushed prices higher; in Western Europe gas-linked pricing amplified the 2022 shock.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Grid capex pass-through and gas-marginal pricing keep European power costs structurally high.
insights.locator: Since 2010, industrial electricity has become more expensive

insights.claim: About $290 billion of German MVA is at risk of relocating if the current competitiveness gap persists, and with US/China-level electricity prices $110 billion of it could match the costs of China-based competitors serving Germany.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: German industrial base is acutely sensitive to energy-price policy; power price reform is a key catalyst.
insights.locator: Germany provides a useful example of what is at stake

insights.claim: Roughly one-third of German industrial manufacturers are moving production capacity abroad because of energy prices, as are nearly one in ten UK manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Energy-driven capacity flight is already underway in Germany and the UK, not hypothetical.
insights.quote: roughly one-third of German industrial manufacturers are moving production capacity abroad because of energy prices
insights.locator: High energy costs already influence investment decisions

insights.claim: With no productivity improvement, an energy-price divergence scenario versus convergence would shift MVA toward China (+$407 billion) and the US (+$151 billion) and away from Western Europe (-$173 billion) and Japan (-$95 billion).
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Energy-rich regions (US, China) are relative winners if power prices diverge further.
insights.locator: Those decisions may prove well-founded

insights.claim: Within Europe, countries with cheap hydroelectric or nuclear power, particularly the Nordic region, would be better positioned than Germany and the UK.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Favor Nordic manufacturing locations and assets over German/UK peers under energy stress.
insights.locator: The effects would also vary considerably within regions

insights.claim: Automation narrows energy disadvantages: in the medium productivity scenario, Western Europe's MVA gap between energy divergence and convergence shrinks from about $173 billion to $77 billion, and it virtually disappears in the most optimistic technology scenario.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Automation and resource efficiency partially hedge European industry against energy price risk.
insights.locator: Technology, however, could change how much these energy cost differences matter

insights.claim: Technology cannot eliminate the importance of energy: in energy-intensive industries such as steel and chemicals, electricity costs may still determine viability even in highly automated factories.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Energy-intensive European producers remain structurally challenged regardless of automation.
insights.locator: In any event, technology cannot eliminate

insights.claim: Data centers accounted for 46% of total market charges across PJM's last four capacity auctions as prices rose from $29 to more than $300 per megawatt-day, meaning manufacturers compete with AI for increasingly expensive electricity.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: AI power demand is a direct cost headwind for US industrial users; watch PJM capacity prices.
insights.quote: Manufacturers therefore face the double challenge of using technology to offset high energy costs while competing with that same technology for increasingly expensive electricity.
insights.locator: In any event, technology cannot eliminate

insights.claim: Manufacturers should make technology and footprint decisions together, determining what FoF modernization level makes each location competitive and when upgrading an existing plant beats moving production.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Expect capex mixes shifting from relocation toward in-place plant upgrades.
insights.locator: What Manufacturers and Policymakers Can Do

insights.claim: Manufacturers should plan for long-term competitiveness rather than the latest disruption, avoiding costly, hard-to-reverse investments made in response to temporary trade or energy shocks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of reactive footprint moves announced in response to short-term tariffs.
insights.locator: Plan for long-term competitiveness, not the latest disruption

insights.claim: Policymakers should accelerate FoF adoption, strengthen workforce skills and digital infrastructure, and ensure costs of expanding grids for AI and electrification do not fall disproportionately on industrial users.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Watch for grid-cost allocation reforms that favor industrial power users.
insights.locator: Invest in the foundations of lasting competitiveness

insights.claim: For strategic sectors such as steel, chemicals and cement that supply defense, infrastructure or technology, resilience may justify local production even where FoF investment cannot make it viable, ideally with support conditioned on modernization.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Strategic heavy industries are likely to receive conditional state support rather than be left to market forces.
insights.locator: Protect strategic sectors where technology alone cannot close the cost gap

insights.claim: Global MVA could rise from $16 trillion today to $26 trillion by 2050, and current decisions by manufacturers and policymakers will help determine where that growth lands.
insights.speaker: Daniel Kuepper
insights.so_what: Large incremental manufacturing pool up for grabs; location competitiveness drives long-run regional industrial growth.
insights.locator: Technology has the potential to alter the economics
